basing-tips.name: Alien world ground
basing-tips.summary: Mixed textures flooded with bright inks, with odd plants and coloured tufts
materials: Fine sand paste, crackle paint and coarse grit paste
Spare tentacles or tails for strange plants
howto: Glue cork down, then spread patches of sand paste, crackle and coarse grit so they overlap.
Press in a few rocks and glue spare tentacles upright in a cluster as an odd plant.
Prime it all white, then flood bright inks into each other while wet so the colours run and mix.
Drybrush white over the raised texture and work a purple wash into dips and round the plants.
Glue on bright tufts, open their tips with tweezers, then varnish matt, as inks dry shiny.

paintSteps.note: A white start keeps the inks bright.
Splash turquoise, purple and magenta wet into each other.
Only once the inks are fully dry.
Into level changes and under plants to separate them.

basing-tips.name: Grey ash wasteland
basing-tips.summary: Dead grey ash drifting over dark rocks and half buried scrap
materials: Bark pieces or slate chips for dark rock
Sand and a few small stones
Small scrap bits such as canisters or pipes
howto: Glue the bark rocks and scrap down first, leaving room for the feet.
Spread fine texture paste thickly over the open ground and bank it up against the rocks and scrap.
Press sand and stones into the wet paste, then dab it with a damp sponge after a while for soft drifts.
Let it dry overnight, paint the rocks near black and wash the ground with a thin grey mix.
Drybrush a warm white very lightly, then add a few dry grass clumps and paint the rim black.

paintSteps.note: Rocks only, with a broken edge where the ash meets them.
Grey thinned right down with water and a drop of matt varnish.
Dot it into tracks and hollows while the grey is still wet.
A very light dusting for the pale flecks in ash.

basing-tips.name: Bark rocks
basing-tips.summary: Garden bark or cork bark chips as layered, wind worn rocks and riverbeds
materials: Garden bark chips or real cork bark
A pin vice and brass rod
howto: Break the bark into pieces of different sizes, as its flaky layers read like wind worn rock.
Plan the rocks while building the model so the feet still fit, then super glue them down.
If a figure stands on a rock, pin through foot, rock and base, as glue alone can snap.
For a riverbed, roll leftover putty into smooth pebbles and scatter sand between them.
Fill any gaps a brush could not reach later with extra small rocks before priming.

paintSteps.note: Right into every layer of the bark.
Firm strokes across the layers to pick them out.
Light, on the top edge of each layer only.

basing-tips.name: Beach shoreline
basing-tips.summary: A sandy shore with driftwood and tiny shells half buried
materials: Small pieces of driftwood or twigs
howto: Paint glue in a rough patch where the sand should go and leave some ground bare.
For wind ripples, first drag a flat shaper through a thin layer of putty in wavy, crossing lines.
Dip the base in sand, tap off the loose grains, and glue driftwood and props in so they look half buried.
Once painted, run clear water gel along the lowest edge for lapping surf.
Keep the base darker overall and the props few, so it does not draw the eye from the model.

paintSteps.note: Cover the sand and the bare ground.
Into the gaps and round the props.
Light, on the sand only, from one side so ripples catch it.
Wood and shells picked out after the sand.
On the low side where the water gel will sit.

basing-tips.name: Mixed ground
basing-tips.summary: Rocks, sand and cracked earth feathered into one natural ground
materials: A few small rocks or slate pieces
Sand and grit in fine, medium and coarse sizes
White glue and a damp old brush
howto: Plan where the feet go, then glue rocks at random rather than in a neat ring, with a tiny root on any bank.
Lay at least two textures, such as sand and crackle, with grit of three sizes in overlapping patches.
Add the second paste while the first is wet, or feather the joins with a damp brush, so no line shows.
Paint one colour over every texture so they read as one ground, then wash and drybrush as normal.
Shade round the foot of each rock with thinned dark brown and soften the line with a damp brush.

paintSteps.note: One colour over everything ties the textures together.
Let it settle in the gaps and at the foot of the rocks.
Over the whole base to bring out every texture.
Light touches on the high points only, brushed in circles.

basing-tips.name: Classic bright green base
basing-tips.summary: Old style sand soaked in bright green and drybrushed yellow for a retro look
howto: Fill any loose slot round the model's tab with putty so the glue has something to sit on.
Brush white glue over the base top, dip it in sand, tap off the excess and wipe the rim clean with a thumb.
Leave it an hour, then soak very watery green into the sand so it runs into every grain.
Once dry, drybrush bright yellow in light flicks across the grains, steering round the feet.
Paint the rim in the same green, less thinned, with smooth strokes.

paintSteps.note: Thinned with lots of water so the sand soaks it up.
Light flicks across the tops of the grains.
For the rim, smooth and less thinned.

basing-tips.name: Cobblestone streets
basing-tips.summary: Putty cobbles pressed into a street, with mud and town debris in the gaps
materials: Silicone shapers, an old damp brush or a cobble texture roller
Fine dirt and thin super glue
Small debris such as bones, pots or scrap wood
howto: Spread a thin layer of putty and press in stone shapes, or roll a cobble texture roller across it in one even pass.
Push the gaps down with a damp brush or shaper so each stone stands proud of the next.
Trim the edges after about an hour, let it cure, then sand a few stones flat for wear.
Scatter dirt and debris, seal it with thin super glue and blot the excess with paper towel at once.
Prime and paint, then add tufts and flowers in the gaps to hide any messy patches.

paintSteps.note: Thin it a little and vary the grey from stone to stone.
Over the dirt between the stones for quick depth.
Thin layers in the gaps so the stones look grimy.
A few stone edges only, adding more khaki for the last pass.

basing-tips.name: Blood and slime pools
basing-tips.summary: Glossy blood, slime or glowing ooze pooled in the hollows of a base
materials: Thick clear gloss water effect or clear resin
Clear tinting inks or see-through paints in red, green or yellow
Tiny glass beads or silica beads for bubbles
A toothpick or silicone shaping tool
howto: Paint the hollow first, dark for blood and murky slime and bright yellow under ooze that should glow.
Glaze the pool bed with ink so it reads deeper in the middle and lighter at the edges.
Stir a very small drop of ink into the clear gloss and pour it in thin layers, as it shrinks while drying.
While the last layer is wet, drop in a few tiny beads so they sink halfway and look like bubbles.
Dot a brighter tint round the bubbles once cured, then add dead tufts along the edge.

paintSteps.note: Under glowing ooze, so the green on top looks lit from within.
Over the yellow, darker towards the middle of the pool.
For blood, glaze over a pale bed so it deepens away from the edge.
Blend the ground into the pool edge so it looks stained.

basing-tips.name: Paving and cast stone
basing-tips.summary: Cracked paving from snapped tile and grout, or cast stone from paste
materials: A plain plastic floor tile with no sticky back
Grey texture paste, for cast stone
Gravel and a few small grass tufts
howto: Snap the tile by hand or with pliers, as it breaks with rough edges much like real paving.
Glue the pieces down as one cracked slab, or tilt and prop some up as if the ground has shifted.
Press in gravel, then fill the gaps with sanded grout straight from the tube and shape it with the stick.
For cast stone walls or floors, spread grey texture paste unevenly with a spatula, not a brush.
Once painted, add a little grass in the cracks for an overgrown look.

paintSteps.note: Over the slabs, though grey paste already gives this colour.
On the grout and ground between the slabs.
Thin, low down, in the cracks and along the edges.
Wipe the brush almost dry or the texture flattens.
Only on slab edges and broken corners.

basing-tips.name: Cork and texture gel
basing-tips.summary: Broken cork under coarse gel for quick, rocky earth
materials: Coarse sheet cork with large, loose grains
A pin and an old brush
howto: Tear coarse sheet cork into rocks by twisting pliers in it, as fine pressed cork looks like cork, not stone.
Trim each piece flat underneath, glue it down, and gouge any smooth cork faces with a pin.
Spread texture gel round the cork so it slopes down to the base, pressing grit into it while wet.
Let it dry fully, then prime, as the primer seals the cork well enough to paint.
Keep spare corks, as a stack of them makes a simple holder for painting models.

paintSteps.note: Cover the cork and gel completely.
Bring out the torn edges of the cork rocks.
Light pass on the highest edges.

basing-tips.name: Crackle paint earth
basing-tips.summary: Crackle paint blended into sand for sun baked cracked ground
materials: Gritty texture paste or fine sand
An old brush and a damp brush
Two-part epoxy putty, for crisper cracks
howto: Lay a thin coat of sandy paste or brown paint first, so cracks do not open onto bare plastic.
Mix a little grit into the crackle and lay it thicker for bigger cracks, but too thick and it chips off.
Blend it into the sand with a damp brush, push rocks into the sandy parts, and let it dry fully.
Seal the dry crackle with varnish or thinned white glue so washes do not loosen it and chunks stay put.
For crisper cracks, press a very thin rolled sheet of putty over a bumpy base and crack it with a brush end.

paintSteps.note: Thin it a little so it does not fill the cracks.
Sparingly into the cracks, with a darker wash in the deepest ones.
Many light passes, crackle needs more than sand.
Very thin near rocks, then drybrush again.

basing-tips.name: Crystal and ice shards
basing-tips.summary: Jagged ice or crystal shards cut from clear frame plastic or clear rod
materials: Clear plastic frame offcuts or clear acrylic rod
Clippers, a hobby knife and a fine saw
Crackle or rough texture paint for the ground
A hot glue gun and baking paper, for icicles
howto: Cut clear frame or rod into strips and cut both ends at sharp angles so each shard comes to a point.
Shave the sides unevenly with a knife, then glue the shards in leaning clusters of mixed sizes.
Spread texture paint on the ground, wipe any off the feet, and seal it with gloss varnish once dry.
Leave clear plastic bare for glassy crystal, or paint it white and tint it blue, then pile snow round each foot.
For icicles, pull hot glue to a point on baking paper, glue them to bare plastic, not paint, and seal with gloss.

paintSteps.note: Over the ground and any shards meant to look like solid ice.
Neat on the shards, thinned well with medium on the ground.
Wipe most off the brush and dot it into the middle of each shard.
One light pass over everything before the snow goes on.

basing-tips.name: Dirt roads
basing-tips.summary: Rutted dirt tracks pressed into putty and dusted with pigment
materials: Two-part epoxy putty or a thick texture paste
Spare vehicle track links and a toothpick
Fine real earth, white glue and water
Earth pigments in two or three tones
White spirit or pigment fixer and a large soft brush
howto: Lay putty in a road across the base with low banks either side, keeping it below the rim.
While soft, press track links along it and scratch thin wheel ruts with a toothpick.
Spread equal parts earth, white glue and water on the banks so they look rougher than the road.
Once painted, brush dry pigment over the road, wet it with spirit, then dust on a second layer.
Push darker pigment into the ruts and set shrubs in uneven numbers along the banks.

paintSteps.note: Patch in a darker and a lighter earth here and there for variety.
Run it along the ruts and track marks.
Across the road and banks, keeping the ruts dark.
Dry pigment over the road, fixed and then dusted again.

basing-tips.name: Dry mud ground
basing-tips.summary: A quick dried mud texture with a drybrush and grass fibres
materials: Dark brown or black for the rim
howto: Spread texture paste front and back, thinned a little if it looks crusty, and work it round the feet with a wet brush.
Once dry, drybrush the texture with a light earth colour.
Stab the same colour onto the boots, or thin it into low cloth folds, as dried mud spatter.
Push pigment into the hollows and wipe the high points with a damp brush so dust sits only in the dips.
Paint the rim, then dot glue in a few small clumps, dip in grass fibres and pull off any extra with tweezers.

paintSteps.note: Only if the paste dried flat in colour.
Over the texture and onto the boots.
Neat coats on the rim.

basing-tips.name: Dungeon flagstones
basing-tips.summary: Dark, damp stone flags for dungeon and indoor scenes
materials: A grey undercoat and black rim paint
A small soft drybrush and matt varnish
Fine sand or a thinned earth texture paint
howto: Prime grey, paint the stones dark grey up to the feet, and tint a few single slabs a little warmer or cooler.
For worn joints, brush thinned earth texture or fine sand over the stones so it settles in the gaps.
Wash brown and green at the same time, swapping at random so they mix into a damp, mossy look.
Let the wash dry fully, then wipe almost all paint off the brush before drybrushing the fine texture.
Paint the rim matt black and seal with matt varnish to take the shine off the washes.

paintSteps.note: Even coat over all the stone.
Let the two washes mix on the stone.
Very little paint on the brush.
A very light dusting to finish.

basing-tips.name: Dusty wasteland
basing-tips.summary: Dry dusty earth with a rust wash, pigment and dry tufts
materials: Sandy texture paste or fine dry earth
Earth pigment, or scraped soft pastel, in a dark, mid and light tone
howto: Spread texture paste over the base, thinning it with water near the feet, and let it dry fully.
Wash it all with a thinned rust or brown, with two drops of matt varnish stirred in so it dries flat.
Drybrush bone over the texture, or a dark grey for a sooty, burnt look.
Dab on pigment, mostly dark, less mid and a touch of light, carry it up the feet and fix it with a little water.
Stick a few dry tufts on at random, not in rows, paint the rim brown and seal with matt varnish.

paintSteps.note: Over all the texture, thinned with water.
Dot it into the first wash while wet to mottle the ground.
Pick out the raised grit, or use a pale skin tone for a softer finish.
Pigment on the ground and the lower legs.

basing-tips.name: Foam bushes and shrubs
basing-tips.summary: Crumbled sponge mixed with glue and paint into bushes with real height
materials: Fine sponge or soft foam, torn into crumbs
Green and a little yellow paint, thinned with water
An old brush with a blunt handle end
A few tufts to sit round the bushes
howto: Tear the sponge into small crumbs rather than cutting it, so the edges look leafy.
Mix the crumbs with white glue and well thinned paint into a thick paste that holds together.
Lift some on the brush handle, set it on the base and press it into shape with the blunt end.
Build each bush up in clumps for height, as loose crumbs sprinkled on glue only lie flat.
Let the wet paint tint the ground round each bush, and keep colours muted so they do not pull the eye.

paintSteps.note: Mixed into the paste, so the bush is coloured as it goes on.
Over the top of each bush once fully dry.
Lightly on the highest crumbs only.

basing-tips.name: Foam hills and cliffs
basing-tips.summary: Expanding foam carved into light hills and cliffs for display boards
materials: A can of expanding foam, or sheets of extruded foam board
A long snap-off blade knife and a fine hobby knife
howto: Spray foam where hills should go, using less than you think as it grows, or stack cut foam board layers.
Carve slopes and cliff faces with the long blade in several passes, changing blades often.
Slice cracks with a fine knife first, then widen them with a blunt tool so the foam does not tear.
Spread fine filler over the bubbles and steps, then coat it in matt sealer mixed with black, not plain white glue.
Paint it and add trees, bushes and tufts, but never put super glue on bare foam, as it melts it.

paintSteps.note: Cover all the filler.
Over the rock faces to bring out texture.
Into hollows and on tops for moss.

basing-tips.name: Forest floor
basing-tips.summary: Bark, soil, moss and leaves built up with height for woodland
materials: Bark, cork or small rocks for the big shapes
Crumbled dried leaves, birch seeds or tea leaves, and moss clumps
A small twig for a fallen branch
howto: Press putty onto the base for height and shape it with wet fingers, pushing in any bits to half bury them.
Glue the biggest bark or rock pieces first, then smaller stones, then soil, always big to small.
Glue a twig across one side as a fallen branch and settle it into the ground.
Scatter soil and leaf litter, or set single leaves with tweezers, and lock it with thin super glue.
Once painted, add moss, bent paper ferns and tufts in clusters with white glue, against rocks and in hollows.

paintSteps.note: The darkest tone, mixed a little into every earth colour too.
Build up, getting brighter as you go.
Only the raised areas and the moss.
Branch and bark, with a little green in the brown.
Stippled onto rocks for fine moss, never over the whole base.

basing-tips.name: Glowing sewer
basing-tips.summary: Blue-grey sewer stone with rusty grates and glowing green sludge
materials: Stone or brick sewer base toppers
A blue-black acrylic ink and a teal paint
Dark oil paint and white spirit
White, a fluorescent paint in bright green and a little yellow
howto: Prime it all black, dust white from above, then line the brick joints with a thin dark wash.
Glaze a see-through blue-black over the stone, then stipple teal on with a wiped big brush.
Oil wash the stone dark, wipe the tops after half an hour or so, then stipple teal again.
Paint the sludge white first, then fluorescent paint in bright green with a touch of yellow over it.
Paint grates steel, add rust dabs, and rub rust pigment into cracks and along the metal.

paintSteps.note: See-through, so the light undercoat varies it.
Stab straight down, dragging gives streaks.
Over white so it stays bright.
Tiny dabs on rivets and grate edges.

basing-tips.name: Grey rocky ground
basing-tips.summary: A dark textured base drybrushed up to grey with a touch of rust
materials: Textured paste or sand and small rocks
Rust coloured pigment powder and a few grass tufts
howto: Texture with paste, or stones first and then fine sand on thinned white glue, keeping clear of the feet.
Base everything black or dark brown, getting right into every gap so they read as shadow.
Drybrush the whole base dark grey, then paler greys in stages on the raised rocks.
For variety, wash one part of the base black and another brown, then drybrush the pale grey back over it.
Work a little rust pigment in round the rocks, then add a few tufts to hide any patches where grit fell off.

paintSteps.note: Solid over all the texture.
Over everything.
Lighter, on the raised rocks, with a little blue to keep the grey cool.
Very light, only the sharpest edges.

basing-tips.name: Meadow and flowers
basing-tips.summary: Stained sand under layered tufts and flowers for green grassland
materials: Sieved sand in mixed grain sizes
Tweezers and a few dried real grass stems
howto: Glue sand over the base, tap off the extra and wipe the rim clean with a finger.
Once dry, flood on a very thin brown, then drybrush pale bone and paint the rim before any grass.
Glue tufts from low to high, shrubs first, flowers overlapping them, then grass in the gaps.
Dab glue in patches and press grass fibres on, then tap off the loose ones.
Add a few real grass stems, dried flat for a week, and stipple red and green pigment on bare ground.

paintSteps.note: Thin as ink and flooded into the sand.
Light, with the brush wiped almost dry.
For the rim, before the grass goes on.

basing-tips.name: Natural tufts
basing-tips.summary: Cut, tint and tuck tufts so they look rooted, not stuck on
materials: Ready-made grass tufts in two shades and sizes
A one-coat paint in a muted green or straw
A sharp hobby knife and tweezers
A brown shade and a pale paint
howto: Tint bright, plastic-looking tufts on their backing sheet with a one-coat paint and let them dry.
Pull off stray fibres, then cut each tuft in half from the side so a flat edge sits against rocks and walls.
Dip each tuft in glue and push it hard into cracks, corners and dips where water would gather.
Put the tallest in shelter and a few tiny ones in the open, with only a few on ruined or muddy bases.
Dab thinned brown into the roots, stroke pale colour over the tips, then flow watery pigment round the roots.

paintSteps.note: Poke it into the root of the tuft until it soaks in.
Stroke the tips only, using the same highlight as the rocks.
Use the base colour so the tuft looks grown in.

basing-tips.name: Pale dusty stone
basing-tips.summary: Light sandy stone with grimy edges and dust matched on the feet
materials: Brown oil paint and odourless spirits
A soft make-up brush for the last drybrush
howto: Base the ground brown, then build up through lighter browns to ivory, brighter than feels right.
Sponge a dark greenish brown grime onto the edges of the base.
Wash with thinned oil paint, then wipe back with clean spirits where the stone should be brightest.
Mix pigment with water, run it round the feet and dry it with a hair dryer.
Dab dry pigment onto the feet and lower legs so model and ground share the same dust.

paintSteps.note: Solid coat over the whole ground.
Over most of the base.
Strong, as the wash tones it down, with a soft brush to spare the edges.
Edges of the base only.
Wipe it back on the brightest stone, or use a yellow-brown for a sunnier stone.

basing-tips.name: Paper plants
basing-tips.summary: Laser cut paper ferns and leaves shaped, tinted and glued in natural clumps
materials: A blunt point such as a ball tool
Strong hair gel, to stiffen shaped leaves
A green shade and a soft brown shade
howto: Pop each plant out of the sheet gently, using tweezers for small bits left in the frame.
Bend and twist every plant so none sit flat, opening healthy leaves out and letting dead ones droop and curl.
Run a blunt point down a leaf so its sides lift, or roll the tip to curl it, and hair gel holds the shape.
Before gluing, wash live plants green and dead ones soft brown to hide the white cut edges.
Glue ferns first, then larger leaves, then a few tufts, letting them hide joins and spill over rocks.

paintSteps.note: Thin it well so it tints the print without hiding it.
On dead or dying leaves, and on the tips of a few live ones.
Lightly over the leaf edges while the plant is still loose.

basing-tips.name: Puddles and water
basing-tips.summary: Tinted gloss puddles and water gel in the low parts of a base
materials: Thick gloss varnish or a ready-mixed water gel
A thick water gel for ripples
Two-part clear resin and tape, for deeper water
howto: Paint and finish the ground first, darkening the mud round each dip, as wet earth is darker.
Stir a single drop of tinted paint into thick gloss, blue-green for clean water or yellow-brown for swamp.
Fill the dips in thin layers, popping bubbles with a toothpick, and pull a little out with a wet brush for damp ground.
For deeper water, tape round the base edge and pour two-part resin in layers no more than about 6 mm thick.
Drag water gel into rings round rocks, then gloss over it, which also clears water that cured cloudy or scratched.

paintSteps.note: Darken the bottom of the dip before the gloss goes in.
One drop of paint in the gloss is plenty.
Top coat to level and clear the surface.
A fine shine line where the water meets rock or wood.

basing-tips.name: Real soil and fine dirt
basing-tips.summary: Sifted garden soil fine enough to keep small or sculpted bases crisp
materials: An old blender or mortar for grinding
A nylon stocking or very fine sieve
A tub kept for fine dirt only
howto: Dry the soil fully so it does not clump, grind it fine, pick out stones and twigs, and sift it through a stocking.
Keep a tub of only the finest dirt, as coarse grains look like boulders, and save any tiny roots for later.
Brush thinned white glue over the base, not letting it pool and fill any sculpted detail.
Dip the base into the tub, or spoon dirt over it, and tap off the excess once it grips.
Flow thin super glue over the dirt to seal it if you want to paint straight away.

paintSteps.note: Thinned a little so it soaks into the dirt without clogging it.
Over the whole base to bring out the grain.
Very light, on the highest grains only.

basing-tips.name: Red desert
basing-tips.summary: Dusty red ground and rocks drybrushed from deep red to bone
materials: Cork pieces and small flat slate
howto: Super glue cork and slate on, leaving room for the feet, then prime.
Brush glue round the rocks, leaving some bare patches, dip in sand and wipe the rim clean.
Paint the bare patches dark red brown, since this shows through the cracks later.
Lay crackle thickly on the patches, feather it into the sand with a wet brush, and seal it with varnish once dry.
Drybrush up through the colours without fully cleaning the brush, then dust on pigment and add a few tufts.

paintSteps.note: On rocks and ground.
Shades without killing the red, and a thin dark green deepens the lowest spots.
Rough pass over all the texture.
Lighter, mostly on the rocks.
A very light touch on the highest edges.

basing-tips.name: Red toadstools
basing-tips.summary: Red caps washed brown and drybrushed up on pale stems
materials: Small sculpted or cast toadstools, or putty caps on wire stems
A fine brush and an old brush for drybrushing
A dark brown shade and some clear medium
Moss or small tufts to sit round them
howto: Glue the toadstools in a small cluster of mixed sizes, in shade by a rock, root or tuft.
Paint the stems white and the caps a deep red, keeping the two colours apart.
Wash everything with dark brown thinned half and half with medium, giving the stems a second coat.
Drybrush the caps bright pink-red, then give the tops a gentle pass of pale pink.
Dot a few pale spots on the caps if you like, then tuck moss or tufts round the stems.

paintSteps.note: Stems first, with a fine brush.
Caps only.
Half and half with medium, with two coats on the stems.
All over the caps.
A gentle last pass on the top of each cap.

basing-tips.name: Deep resin ice
basing-tips.summary: Clear resin over a mirror and tint, with cracks for real depth
materials: Thin stick-on plastic mirror cut to the base shape
Clear UV curing resin and a UV lamp
Thinned blue and blue-black one-coat paints
A tiny touch of white paint, for frosted ice
howto: Cut the mirror to the base, stick it down, then spread a thin layer of resin to the edge and cure it.
Spray or glaze thin blue in light layers, with blue-black in one area to suggest deep water.
Brush gloss on and work a wet brush over it so it dries cracked, then drag folded sandpaper across for scratches.
For frosted ice, stir far less than a drop of white into clear resin and set it in hollows and at the foot of snow.
Glue the model on and push snow paste round the edges and feet, which also hides resin that crept up them.

paintSteps.note: Build it in light passes so the mirror still shines through.
Only where you want the ice to look deepest.
Brush on to bring the shine back over the tint.

basing-tips.name: Sand and rocks
basing-tips.summary: Warm sand with a few cool grey rocks and tufts, quick for a whole army
materials: Fine sand mixed with a little coarser grit
Small dry tufts or grass fibres
Tweezers and a soft make-up brush
howto: Glue two to four slate pieces of different sizes on each base, with one stray rock away from the cluster.
Brush white glue out from the centre round the rocks, dip in sand and tap off the extra.
Wipe the rim and flick sand off the rocks while wet, then let it dry naturally, as a hair dryer blows grit off.
Drip thinned white glue over loose sand to lock it, then sweep off dust with a soft brush before priming.
Stain, wash and drybrush as below, then add a tuft or two with white glue.

paintSteps.note: Very thin over sand and rocks, the sand soaks it up.
Over the sand only, after a thin wash of black on the rocks.
Over the rocks only, and jabbing it on with an old brush also works.
Light pass over everything to tie it together.
Neat rim, starting and ending at the back.

basing-tips.name: Sandbags and low walls
basing-tips.summary: Putty sandbags laid over a low wall of small stacked stones
materials: Small rounded stones or fine gravel
A little water to stop the putty sticking
howto: Clear the front of the base and stack small stones into a low wall with dots of super glue.
Roll a thin strip of putty, flatten it slightly and cut it into small rectangles.
Lay the bags one at a time over the wall, overlapping like bricks, and press each so it sags naturally.
Press the edge of the knife along each bag to mark the seams and pinch the corners a little.
Let the putty cure fully, then paint the stones and the bags as separate steps.

paintSteps.note: Cover all the stones in the wall.
Two passes pick out the shape of each stone.
On the bags, or a dull olive mixed with ochre works too.
On the tops of the bags only.
Run it along the seams and between the bags to outline them.

basing-tips.name: Sci-fi deck plates
basing-tips.summary: A spaceship floor base from plastic card, tube and fine mesh
materials: A compass cutter and a steel ruler
howto: Measure the top face of the base, which is smaller than its listed size, and cut a disc to match.
Pencil panel lines, cut thin slivers out between panels, glue them down and deepen the lines with a file.
Add tube as pipes and frame offcuts as steps, then file every end flush with the rim.
Lay mesh over the pipes, short of the edges, and hide its cut edges under thin card strips.
Make a dent with a knife tip and drill tiny holes in panel corners as bolts.

paintSteps.note: Keeps everything under the mesh in shadow.
Heavy, buffed onto the panels, brightest just off centre like a spotlight.
Swap between brown and black for uneven grime.
Light pass to catch the panel edges.
Small random patches, kept matt, with a dot of dark gloss for spilt oil.

basing-tips.name: Sea waves
basing-tips.summary: Surf breaking on a cork rock, shaped from fast-setting putty
materials: Cork, even an old bottle stopper, for the rock
Fast-setting two-part putty or a thick water gel
A dental spatula or sculpting tool
howto: Carve and tear cork into a rock with natural edges and glue it over about two thirds of the base.
Knead a small amount of putty until the colour is even and press it onto the open area.
Push it into curling waves with quick, firm strokes, leaving flat room for the feet, as it sets in minutes.
Wash your hands after handling the putty and let it set hard before painting.
Paint the water and the rock, fix the figure on, and add a little grass on top of the rock.

paintSteps.note: The darkest water, left showing in the hollows.
Brush up the wave faces with plenty of paint, mixing lighter each pass.
Only on the crests and where the foam hits the rock.
On the rock, over a dark brown base coat.
On the water only, so it looks wet against the matt rock.

basing-tips.name: Slate shards
basing-tips.summary: Real slate pushed up through the earth for broken, burst ground
materials: A natural slate tile broken with a hammer
Earth texture paste or two-part epoxy putty
howto: Wrap the slate in a cloth before you hit it, then pick the best sharp shards.
Glue the shards so they angle upward, as if the ground has burst open.
Blend the gaps round them with paste or putty and sprinkle soil on while wet, piling more against the shards.
Once dry, lock any loose soil with thinned white glue so it does not shed under the brush.
Paint and wash the whole base, then dab pigments on for colour variation.

paintSteps.note: Dark base over the whole ground.
Over everything, into the slate layers.
Catch the split edges of the shards.
Pigment dabbed on the earth, not the slate.

basing-tips.name: Snow drifts
basing-tips.summary: Gritty white snow over cold blue ground, with rocks pushed bright
materials: Cork pieces and a few small rocks
A light textured modelling paste or ready-mixed snow paste
Fine snow powder and a pinch of pearly sparkle powder
Or white glue thickened with baking soda and a drop of white
An old brush and a pot of water
howto: Glue cork and rocks inside the rim, hide the cork under texture paste, then prime dark grey.
Drybrush the ground cold blues and glue in tufts before any snow, as both show through in the shadows.
Use less than you think, dabbing paste into cracks and against rocks, thick in drifts and thin at the edges.
While wet, sprinkle snow powder and a pinch of sparkle over it and tap off the extra, as the paste acts as glue.
For homemade snow, stir baking soda into white glue until it holds a peak, with a drop of white so it dries bright.

paintSteps.note: Cover the rocks and ground before the snow goes on.
Brush the rocks firmly so their texture shows.
Push rock edges brighter than feels right, as snow makes them read dark.
On bare ground under thin snow, not grey.
Very thin into the undersides of the drifts for shadow.

basing-tips.name: Snowy flagstones
basing-tips.summary: Grey flagstones with tints, dead leaves and blue-shadowed snow
howto: Test-fit the painted model on the base, holding it in tissue, before painting the base.
Paint the stones and ground as below, then pick out leaves and any small details.
Spoon snow paste into drifts with an old brush, leaving room for the feet, and build it up once dry.
While the snow is still wet, touch in a very thin blue so it soaks in as cold shadow.
When fully dry, glue the model on and paint the rim black.

paintSteps.note: On the stone, with warm brown on any earth.
Overbrush the stone, then a thin wash of black over it all.
Flagstone edges and a few scratches.
Thin patches on random stones for age.
Drop into the wet snow for shadow.

basing-tips.name: Grass fibres and scatter
basing-tips.summary: Dipped grass fibres, layered fine scatter and raised moss paste for grassy bases
materials: Grass fibres in two or three shades, and very fine foam scatter
Thin super glue or white glue
A tub of grass fibres for dipping
Dark green paint and paper towel, for moss paste
A balloon and a wool jumper, to lift the fibres
howto: Dot glue in patches on a painted, dry base, leaving bare ground between, dip it in the tub and flick the underside.
For taller grass, dab a clump on wet glue with tweezers and pull away, or hold a charged balloon just above it.
Build in layers, with fine scatter first as low texture, then grass fibres, then a few tufts for bigger clumps.
For raised moss, mix fine scatter with plenty of white glue, a drop of dark green and very little water.
Blot the brush on paper towel, dab the paste where moss grows and press it down, as it grips only once dry.

paintSteps.note: Dulls bright packet green and dirties the roots.
Lightly over the tips once dry, or varnish first to stiffen it for a full repaint.

basing-tips.name: Swamp and bog
basing-tips.summary: Dark wet mud, a murky pond, a mossy log and hanging moss with a gloss finish
materials: Grass tufts and moss pads in several greens
Cotton wool and white glue for hanging moss
Clear gloss wet-effect gel or water effect
A real twig for a log
howto: Dab a thick layer of mud paste on and press tufts, moss pads, a twig log or rocks into it while wet.
Leave a hollow free for a pond and paint its bed dark in the middle, fading to lighter green at the shore.
For hanging moss, soak cotton wool in one part glue to three of water and tease it into strands on plastic.
Once dry, drape the strands over the log and wash them dark green, with a lighter green touched on top.
Run a green shade into the mud for algae, then add gloss gel to the pond and low ground so it looks wet.

paintSteps.note: Pond bed, dark in the deep end blending to grass green at the shore.
Only in the deepest part of the pond.
Into the mud for algae, feathered out at the edges.
Gloss over the matt wash makes the mud read as boggy.

basing-tips.name: Texture paint ground
basing-tips.summary: A quick gritty base spread on with an old brush and tidied
materials: Gritty texture paint, or a large tub of artist's texture paste
An old flat brush or a flexible plastic spatula
Fine grit or a few small stones
A couple of grass tufts and tweezers
howto: Pick a ground that contrasts with the model, light ground for a dark model and dark for a light one.
Blob the paste in the middle and spread it out to the feet, about 1 to 2 mm thick so it suits the scale.
Wipe paste off the feet with a clean damp brush, and press grit in while wet, as the paste acts as glue.
Let it air dry for up to an hour, as a hair dryer can skin the surface, and rinse the brush under a strong tap.
Paint the rim neatly, then press a tuft or two on with tweezers so no grass sticks to wet rim paint.

paintSteps.note: Brings out the grit if the paste came out flat.
Brush firmly with a wide flat brush, as the grit is locked in.
For the rim, painted last.

basing-tips.name: Tile grout ground
basing-tips.summary: Cheap sanded tile grout that grips the base without glue
materials: Sanded tile grout for grit, or unsanded for a smoother ground
A metal palette knife or an old spoon
Brown acrylic ink or a brown shade
Black paint or acrylic ink for the rim
howto: Spread a thin layer of grout over the top of the base with the palette knife, and it sticks without extra glue.
Press in a few small rocks while it is soft, then let it dry, which takes under an hour.
Left plain, its own colour reads as beach sand, so it can be inked straight away.
For darker earth, flood brown acrylic ink over it so the colour soaks right in, and let it dry.
Drybrush a light tan over the grains and paint the rim black for a neat edge.

paintSteps.note: Use plenty so it soaks into the grout.
Catch just the tops of the grains.
On the rim only.

basing-tips.name: Tinted moss
basing-tips.summary: Green tint dropped onto drybrushed rocks for quick moss
materials: A finished, drybrushed rocky or earth base
Fine green scatter and thin super glue, for raised moss
howto: Start from a base that is already painted and drybrushed.
Drop a little light green onto parts of the rocks, mostly on tops and the shaded side.
Push it around with a very wet clean brush so it settles into the texture, adding more for stronger colour.
Once dry, add a darker green the same way in a few places, with a touch of brown in it to look more natural.
Drybrush pale bone lightly to blend, then for raised moss glue fine scatter in cracks and dull it with a brown shade.

paintSteps.note: Let it settle into the texture, as it looks patchy until it dries.
A few patches only, inside the lighter moss.
Very light, to tie moss and rock together.

basing-tips.name: Trees from roots and twigs
basing-tips.summary: Model trees from dried roots and twigs, with putty hiding the joins
materials: Dry roots and twigs in a range of thicknesses
Two-part epoxy putty and a sculpting tool
A pin vice and brass rod for pinning
Clump foliage or sea moss sprigs, and fine scatter
howto: Collect far more dry roots and twigs than you need, and pick a main tree big enough to tower over the figure.
Place the largest tree first, then smaller ones either side to frame the figure, one running past the top.
Glue with super glue and accelerator, one branch at a time, letting each set before the next goes on.
Press putty into the gaps and joins, curing each layer, then drag a tool along the grain so it reads as bark.
Fix foliage with super glue on the twig and white glue between clumps, and pin the figure so it always refits.

paintSteps.note: Over wood and putty so the joins disappear.
Along the grain to bring out the bark.
Lightly on the highest ridges and roots.
Into the roots and shaded side, alternating with thin brown for damp bark.

basing-tips.name: Urban ruins
basing-tips.summary: Ruined city ground of slabs, bricks and rubble in dirty grey
materials: Broken floor slabs or small slate pieces
Plastic frame offcuts cut into bricks, planks and rubble
Sand, white glue and super glue
Rust, red brick and pale dust pigments
howto: Build one focal pile of beams and bricks leaning together, dry fitting the model so the feet sit firm.
Lay broken slabs round it, fill cracks with chopped frame plastic or crushed rubble, the rest with texture paste.
Stain everything a thin grey-brown, then wash brown and olive together without rinsing for grime.
Drybrush the slabs grey and pick out a few bricks in two or three warm tones, starting lighter than you want.
Add rust on metal, red brick dust on broken bricks, then pale dust on the ground and feet, fixed with matt varnish.

paintSteps.note: Heavily thinned over everything.
Over the slabs and sand.
Over the rocks and bricks only.
On beams and metal bits.
Light pass over everything to unify it.

basing-tips.name: Weathered marble
basing-tips.summary: Quick old marble or stone flooring with dirt and a hint of moss
materials: A base with sculpted stone or ruins
A dry wipe stretched tight, for airbrushed veins
howto: Prime it all black and dust grey from above.
Drybrush the stone deep ivory with a circular motion, leaving grey in the recesses.
Paint soil brown, wash brown and green at once, and let it dry fully so the next drybrush does not smear.
Bring the ivory back, dust pale bone over it all, and paint the rim matt black.
For veined marble, airbrush pale greys and white through a wipe stretched tight over the base, then gloss it.

paintSteps.note: Heavy, leaving grey in the recesses.
Mix brown and green on the base for age.
Lighter pass to bring the marble back.
Very light dusting over everything.

basing-tips.name: Wet muddy earth
basing-tips.summary: Glossy churned mud splashed up the boots and worked into tufts and puddles
materials: Wet mud texture paint or a thick brown texture paste
Clear heavy gel with a little dark brown pigment, for glossy mud
A stiff short brush and a toothpick, for splatter
howto: Spread mud thickly round the feet, with a little sand or root bits mixed in, then add more for mounds and ruts.
Thin some with water and stab it onto the boots, or flick it from a stiff brush with a toothpick for spatter.
Press footprint dips into the wet mud with the back of a brush.
Glue on tufts, then brush thinned mud over them so they look trampled rather than fresh.
Once painted, leave raised mud matt and lighter, and gloss the dips and lowest mud so it looks fresh and wet.

paintSteps.note: Over a dark primer, on every base at once so they match.
A firm pass to lift the ridges of the mud.
Over everything for a grimy, slightly mossy tone.
Only in the hollows and on the wettest mud.

basing-tips.name: Wooden plank floors
basing-tips.summary: Weathered wooden planks for ship decks, floors and walkways
materials: Balsa or thin wooden strips in a few widths
A hobby knife and an awl or pin
howto: Glue wooden strips across the base in a few widths, leaving a snapped board or small gaps for interest.
Soak the wood with thin super glue to harden it, then trim the overhang flush with the rim.
Gouge and scratch the planks along the grain and press nail holes near the ends with an awl.
Sand the edge smooth, prime, and paint the planks in slightly different browns or greys.
Wash neighbouring planks with different washes, then wipe the tops back with damp tissue so dirt stays in the gaps.

paintSteps.note: Keeps the gaps between planks dark.
Vary it a little from plank to plank.
Swap to black or grey on the next plank, then wipe the tops back.
Along the grain, not across it.
Into a few low joins and plank ends as algae.

basing-tips.name: Worn grass pitch
basing-tips.summary: Cracked dry earth, tufts and faded white lines like a playing field
materials: A beige brown paint and wash
Grass tufts in two colours, or grass fibres
Masking tape and a small sponge
howto: Paint the base first so any wide cracks do not show bare black.
Mix crackle with a little gritty paste and spread it on, then let it dry fully.
Wash with a beige brown and drybrush the raised chunks.
Stick on tufts in two shades with their tops pressed different ways, or trim grass fibres flat for short turf.
Mask a line and sponge or stipple thick white along it for a worn marking, then paint the rim black.

paintSteps.note: Into all the cracks.
On the raised chunks only.
Broken, patchy line rather than a solid stripe.
